utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I am sorry that some slack technical hitch delayed our start, but we seem to have now all got ourselves present. The purpose this afternoon is to conduct the final Pre-Trial Conference between the parties in preparation for the final commencement tomorrow of the case for the Prosecution. I wonder if the registrar would be kind enough to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-13/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just confirm that each of the accused is able to hear a translation of what is being said in their own language. Mr. Mrksic first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MRKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can hear in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED RADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear and understand everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear everything and everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now have appearances. Firstly, for the Prosecution. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My name is Moore. I'm a Senior Trial Attorney. I'm represented-- or assisted by Ms. Marie Tuma, Mr. Karim Khan Agha, Ms. Merixtell Regue, and Mr. Alex Demirdjian who sit behind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence. Firstly for Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to one and all in the courtroom. The Defence for Mr. Mrksic will be represented by attorney Miroslav Vasic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I hope in due course you will receive assistance, but unfortunately not as you might have hoped.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. We have already taken steps in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now for Mr. Radic, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. The Defence of Miroslav Radic will be represented by myself, Borivoje Borovic, attorney from Belgrade, and co-counsel Mira Tapuskovic, also an attorney from Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. And now for Mr. Sljivancanin, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon to all the participants in the proceedings. The Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin will be represented today by attorneys Novak Lukic and Momcilo Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The parties will be aware but so that it is publicly announced there has been an order made on the 6th of this month assigning the case for trial to this Trial Chamber, and we will be conducting the trial in the months to come. Now, the final Pre-Trial Conference is one for which Rule 73 bis makes provision, and a number of things are there contemplated to be dealt with by the Trial Chamber. I think it fair to say that the parties have felt a little under time pressure in becoming prepared for trial despite what had been earlier understandings and assurances of their trial readiness, so that it is only a matter of some weeks now. I won't embarrass you by saying precisely how many, which I know, that you have had, and in that time there has been quite a deal of adjustment to what had been the case for the Prosecution, and for that reason I think it would not be appropriate at this stage to attempt to finally pin down and make orders about a number of matters that Rule 73 bis contemplates will be finally dealt with at this hearing. I have the impression that it would be fairer for all of you, Prosecution and Defence, if the Chamber is prepared to allow the trial to work its way in a little while you all have time to get more familiar with the new shape of the Prosecution case, and the Prosecution has more time to become clear about its witnesses and the evidence it will lead. Don't take this as a lack of determination on the part of the Chamber to keep things moving efficiently, but you can take heart that it is an indication that we will do our best to ensure that everything works fairly. For that reason, we would, while getting an indication from counsel at this stage about certain matters, we will for the most part be avoiding making any final binding order today despite the normal expectation of the Rule. With that long-winded introduction, Mr. Moore, which I hope will give you a little more comfort and confidence, I now turn to you to inquire as to what you see about the number of witnesses you propose to call and the length of the Prosecution case as you presently anticipate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the comfort. I will endeavour to deal with it as clearly as I can. It is our intention, there are approximately over 80 witnesses at this stage on the Prosecution list. It's certainly our intention to cut that list down significantly. If I may deal with it, I hope, in practical terms, to some extent because of the development of the case there are witnesses that will deal often with scenes or scenarios. It will depend to some extent on the nature of the cross-examination and the issues that will arise, and if that is the case, and I've had full cooperation from my learned friends in relation to that, what I would hope to do is to remove any surplusage on those witnesses that to some extent are extraneous to the matters as a whole. I'm very grateful for the realistic approach taken by the Court and the trust that the Court has placed in all of us, but certainly if I may just give a small example of one of the problems that we have. This trial will be proceeding through November. On the original timetable, it was our intention to call originally Mr. -- or Ambassador Okun and some of the military witnesses, as it were, to start, the experts. The Defence asked for 30 days to consider their evidence. It's a perfectly reasonable request, we accept that, made by the Defence. But additionally many of the witnesses from Vukovar themselves are reluctant, quite understandably you think, to come to court between the 18th and the 25th of November because many of their family have been killed at that time. What we're intending to do, and my learned friends are aware of it and I think are in agreement to it, is that we will start with the crime base witnesses, Dr. Bosanac will be the first witness. We will run those witnesses for a period of three weeks because we have to book, as it were, in advance, and then we will stop that area of evidence and proceed with, I hope, Ambassador Okun, perhaps General Pringle. We don't know exactly how long that will take and then presume, if necessary, on the crime base witnesses after that. At this time we have set aside 15 witnesses to deal with the what I will call the original crime base, namely the incidents at the hospital, running towards Vukovar -- or Velepromet itself. On the time span we think that that is probably achievable. We think at that one witness per day is, I hope, a realistic estimate. Then it equally arises whether the Court are minded, subject obviously to any submissions by my learned friends, whether they are minded to allow us to implement 89(F) for witnesses that may deal with matters that are already covered but do not deny the Defence the ability to cross-examine perhaps on specific issues that may require clarification. And then thirdly to deal with the 92 bis matters. Can I just say in relation to the 92 bis motion it may well be that my learned friends and I will be able to discuss matters throughout this forthcoming two weeks, and it may well be we'll able to narrow the issues down to very clear areas. That is certainly my aim and I suspect my learned friends probably feel the same way. And then perhaps the fourth category relates to the experts and the pathologists. In particular, I have one pathologist in mind whose name completely I forget at this time, but there is a summary of the injuries, the numbers, the causation of the killings at Ovcara, and it may well be that that can be dealt with by way of agreed facts. If it's dealt with by way of agreed facts, I would have thought we would be able to avoid calling or reading three or four expert witnesses. So as far as the Prosecution are concerned, we will deal with crime base first of all, move on to Okun and Pringle, perhaps Theunens, continue with the Ovcara site, and then deal with the JNA military evidence. That is the -- that is the plan that we have at this stage. And as I say, subject obviously to Court's rulings, the Court's views on 89(F) and 92 bis. I hope that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And overall do you have any broad anticipation of the time that will might be needed for the Prosecution case at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I had thought that if I tried to aim for approximately 5/8th, actually I was thinking between 50 and 55 witnesses. If we said approximately a day a witness, that would give, I hope, a sensible estimate of the length of the Prosecution case, which is, I would think, between three and four months. So we would conclude, if we take in the Christmas adjournment, we would conclude I would have hoped by the end of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, that is certainly more ambitious than we had understood and very encouraging. Our last understanding would have put your case at somewhere near six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just say that I really hope that my feet are sufficiently quick to make sure that my -- they are not nailed to the floor, but I will try and deal with this as efficiently and effectively as I can, but I in my mind am going to try and aim for the end of January. But can I ask the Court's indulgence for an element of flexibility on that. Of course the Court may take the view that we are being tremendously dilatory; I don't know. But that is the aim that we have at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Clearly the position that we have when you get to formal proposals on 89(F) and the outcome of the 92 bis motion which I understand has now been filed but which has not yet reached us will have a bearing upon the time that will be taken, and it's not -- there's no way, have no fear, that we could hold you at this moment to any fixed time for completing your case. But to have a general understanding of how long you might see the case is something which will be useful for ourselves and very useful for Defence counsel as they are preparing their case. The object of all of this, as you will understand and as I hope the three accused men will come to understand, is to try and ensure that we finish this case as quickly as fairness will allow, in particular, fairness to be in a position to present your cases with an adequate preparing time to meet the case that is advanced against you. So a quicker finish is desirable, but we keep an eye on fairness. Relevant to that, the Chamber would indicate now first, of course, all will be aware that we have been, while starting the case tomorrow, allowed then a further two weeks effectively to enable some of the difficulties that still exist about pre-trial preparation to be resolved, and in that time we as a Chamber will deal with the 92 bis application and any other matters affecting evidence that need to be dealt with and are ready by that time. We also felt that the Christmas break, the break at late December, early January, would be a time where it would be possible first for the Prosecution to, as it were, give a further reflective consideration to its case and come to some final conclusions perhaps about witnesses that you'd not been able to give full attention to already and to then settle finally your own positions. It would also be a time when the Defence, having by that time heard the Prosecution opening and got into much of their case, would be in a much better position to see your own cases and to be getting your own cases under way in preparation having heard what it is that's coming against you. Because of that, the Chamber was of the mind that it might in fact make a slightly longer than normal break over the January -- December-January period so that both the Prosecution would be fully prepared and the Defence would be in a much better position to get its cases ready. The object of both of those is to try and ensure that the cases for both Prosecution and Defence will be presented as efficiently as possible rather than all the sorts of delays we encounter if people are struggling to be on top of their case. And by allowing a little extra time then, we hope that the overall time for trial will be shorter. And in particular, at the moment I would suggest that you might plan for having the Christmas break, that December break, start one week earlier than the vacation. And that's relevant, of course, to the preparation of the Prosecution witnesses before the break to have that mind that perhaps Friday, the 9th of December, rather than the following Friday, would be a satisfactory time. We in fact lose only three hearing days by doing that because there are two days that would be taken up normally with a Plenary sitting of the Judges so that we wouldn't be sitting then normally. So we will lose three days of sitting but gain five working days of preparation for both Prosecution and Defence. And it may be that a week at the other end, so giving you in effect five weeks work on your cases rather than three, would achieve what we have in mind, and what we have in mind is that the cases for both Prosecution and each one of the Defence, accused, will be able to proceed smoothly and efficiently without wasting of time. We hope that way we can get the estimated time for the total conducting of this trial reduced by quite a considerable amount. In that extra time for preparation, both the two weeks now after the opening and then what could well be two weeks extra over the December-January break, we would hope in particular that a great deal of attention could be given by counsel both for the Prosecution and the Defence to what are the issues that can be resolved between them and agreed or either agreeing facts or agreeing that they really no longer are an issue that's important in the case so that they can be put aside so that everybody's attention can be concentrated on the things that really matter in this case. That might, I hope, Mr. Moore, assist you also in your planning for the time between now and the break in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I had omitted, of course, the two weeks in October, and if we have those additional breaks, and in my submission it's a very good idea to have that slightly longer period over Christmas, I would think there would be a realistic prospect of finishing then by the end of February. I'll see what my learned friends say about that, but we're perfectly agreeable to the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I trust all counsel will realise this isn't suggesting you should have two extra weeks skiing. The Chamber is hoping there will be two extra weeks of very profitable work and negotiation between the parties, and that's what is in mind. The number of documentary exhibits, Mr. Moore, at the moment there seems a very large number, is that subject to revision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be. The exhibits themselves really break into three categories. The first principal category are military exhibits created by the military analyst Mr. Theunens. I have spoken to him about these exhibits, and I've asked whether it's possible to bring them down to a significant -- significantly and to a more manageable number for several reasons. One of them is because we're no longer going into E-court and we're work off paper, and therefore it would be my intention for the Court and everybody to have what I will call a large folder of hard copy exhibits. So those -- I think there are 400 exhibits actually generated by him. I'm not quite sure of the figure but I think it's fairly close to that. The second category of exhibits relates to the analysis, the pathology analysis. I suspect that we can reach some form of agreement in relation to that. I can't for my life imagine that the Defence are going to take any great issue on that, but perhaps they can clarify that. And then thirdly there are what I call general exhibits thrown up by either the witness statement itself, or some of the witnesses here have given evidence in Dokmanovic and Milosevic and often there have been exhibits that come from those trials. Again, it is our aim, and we've already started doing it, to try and slimline the exhibits itself. But in relation to the first two categories, I would have thought that we could have made significant inroads into those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could I turn from you, Mr. Moore, to -- firstly to Mr. Vasic. The -- quite a bit has been said about the anticipated progress of the trial, how it might be managed with time and the length of the Prosecution case. Is there anything at this point that you would like to add about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. All I can say is that, rest assured, that the Defence will not go off on a winter holiday, because we'd all like this to be as expeditious as possible. And I highly respect and value the words of my learned friend of the Prosecution. However, I do feel that the programme that was set out by the Prosecution for the examination-in-chief of witnesses in view of the Defence is shorter than would be realistic, and I say that for this reason: The Defence analysed some of the documents that it received from the Prosecution, and we can conclude that quite a large number of witnesses have already testified in four proceedings before different courts. So that's a specific feature of this particular case. We have not encountered an example of that kind before here at the Tribunal, and I consider that that fact in the examination-in-chief if not by my colleague of the Prosecution then in cross-examination by the Defence teams will require longer time for matters to be dealt with that are contained in witness statements in order to get the necessary explanations and reasonable ones. And I think that that must be borne in mind when we talk about how many witnesses we can get through per day. I also hope that both sides will do their utmost to be as efficient as possible, given the time available. The other matter that my learned colleague mentioned has to do with the proposal made by the Prosecution in the 92 bis motion, and it received this motion on Friday. So we'll be able to state our views within the deadline as provided for by the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, and the Defence will present its positions and say which witnesses it agrees to have heard under 92 bis and which it does not or, rather, for which it will require cross-examination. The next point is 89(F), Rule 89(F), and I would like to understand it that the proposal made by my learned colleague goes along the lines of what is provided for by the Rules, and that is that Rule 89(F) is indeed an exception of the rule of the presentation -- governing the presentation of evidence in these proceedings and that before this Trial Chamber we shall indeed treat it as an exception with each individual case looked at separately. And finally, the Defence for its side will say that it will do its best to meet its obligations, to protect their client's interests in the best possible way. And since we're still not in a position to be able to give you a complete picture of what we intend to do once we have got -- receive the material from the Prosecution, that's as far as I will go here today. That's what I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, thank you for that -- I'm sorry. I trust your client will forgive me. Mr. Vasic. There are two observations. First, the fact that you may have a number of transcripts of previous testimony of witnesses available which could well assist in your cross-examination. Could we point out that it may also assist in being able to agree certain matters. If you can see from those transcripts clearly that certain issues are well held and well supported so that it may well be a means of reducing time. And of course if one counsel goes through and explores an area from a past transcript, there ought not to be need for other Defence counsel to go over the same ground for the same purpose. If you would just have that in mind. But the second point, I noticed from the Defence pre-trial position that it appeared that all Prosecution exhibits were to be questioned for authenticity. Now, I hope I misunderstood or misread, but if that is the position that has been tentatively taken, I would certainly, speaking for the Chamber, encourage you and the other two Defence teams to look again, because there must be a large number of those documents that you really are not questioning for authenticity. So please have in mind that when you have this next two weeks to be working on the case that those documents, many of them, are documents which you may want to question some point about but you're not saying this is a forgery, this is a false document, this is a document that isn't a genuine one, whereas the impression that I got from reading what have been put forward suggested you were going to be challenging every document as not authentic. Perhaps you had just bear that in mind. No need to comment on it now. Now, Mr. -- is there something you'd like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few sentences, if I may. As far as the documents are concerned, the Defence in its -- wrote its pre-trial motions under circumstances well known to the Trial Chamber, that is to say, we still did not have most of the material to be disclosed to us by the Prosecution. So the Defence will at all events together with -- cooperate with our learned friends of the Prosecution with respect to determining the authenticity of the documents and their truthfulness to the original. You need have no doubts on that score. Of course, the Defence won't question all the documents tendered by the Prosecution. That would have no sense at all. Now, as far as the previous position is concerned, the position with respect to the witness testimony and transcripts that we have, I am in full agreement that the witness statements and testimony in the transcripts helps us to know what individual witnesses said on occasion, but this also opens up the inconsistency in various witnesses based on the transcripts. So the Defence will need time to go through all those sections in the transcript to be able to establish the authenticity of the witness testimonies. Now, as far as your concern about the fact that the Defence will repeated itself, repeat questions and issues, I hope that won't happen. We always did so up still now together on the basis of joint motions, so I hope that we'll be efficient in preparing for the trial. That's what I wanted to say. Thank you. Just to tell you that the Defence will not do anything that might be seen as an abuse and prolongation of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Vasic, yes. Mr. Borovic, is there anything that you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are thankful to the Defence of Miroslav Radic and the efforts of this Trial Chamber to extend our deadlines which will raise the quality of our defence for our client. Not only will be able to assess the evidence, both of the Prosecution and the Defence, but this will be in the interests of justice, and we'll be able to see what the Prosecution has laid at our feet so that we can react. As far as 92 bis is concerned, this Defence counsel will set out our positions in writing. We do have certain reservations with respect to what the Prosecution said but we shall do so in writing. The order of witnesses as proposed by the Prosecution is quite all right. We shall need more time. We are doing our best to read through the material very quickly, and we came in early today to collect up all the documents. Now, with respect to the question you asked of the representative of the first Defence team, that is of Mr. Mrksic, whether the large number of statements which are repeated in different trials and proceedings will accelerate and facilitate the criminal proceedings, this will be as follows: In the cross-examination, we of the Defence counsel will extend that time because we listen carefully to the statements and testimony made in different proceedings and reached the conclusion that they are in collision with each other, sometimes completely so. I don't want to bring them up now, but that will be the proper time to cross-examine ten or 15 important witnesses. All the rest, everything else, this Defence team will of course try to get through in the briefest possible time to be efficient. Our clients have been in detention for a long period of time, and they are very pleased to see that the trial will go ahead. And this trial, of course, realise on a series of other proceedings pertaining to the same criminal act, so that it will be interesting to see this sword match between the Prosecution and the Defence, and I'm sure that this Trial Chamber, judging by the initial steps, will, I'm sure, be able to assess the matter in the right way in the interests of justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic, is there anything you would want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't wish to repeat what my colleagues have just said. Would I just like to follow on from what they have stated and raise a practical matter. I'd like to ask this Honourable Trial Chamber for its assistance, although I have already discussed the matter with my colleague of the Prosecution. Precisely because of the situation we're faced with and Mr. Vasic informed you of that situation, that is to say, the vast amount of material for each witness to come into court, it would mean a great deal to us in preparing our Defence cases if we were to be informed in a timely fashion of the order of witnesses, the order in which the witnesses will be taken for, let's say, a two-week period, on the basis of a fortnightly period. Then we will be able to divide up our work with the individual witnesses, and I don't suppose that the Prosecution will mind. They have told us of the first witness, but if they could always let us know a fortnight in advance what the order of witnesses is, the witnesses they intend to call. So that would mean a great deal to the Defence teams, and we would of course have the same obligation in the Defence case to send in list of witnesses and order of witnesses to the Prosecution. Of course I know that this order can change from time to time, but to have the basic structure set out well in advance. And it would be a good idea perhaps if we were to hear the Trial Chamber's instructions along those lines, and guidelines. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, then, Mr. Lukic. We will come to that just a little later, your specific proposal. Could I ask now to understand, Mr. Moore, the position about disclosure. Has both Rule 66 and Rule 68 now been satisfied?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My Lord, as far as we're aware, we have fulfilled all our obligations on Rule 66. Rule 68, all disclosure is an ongoing operation, but at this time we have disclosed all matters that are relevant in respect of this case. But we are, as I say, continuing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My Lord, may I just interrupt for one short moment in relation to the submission that my learned friend Mr. Lukic made about the witnesses being two weeks ahead. For our part, we will try and do that, as long as there is a clear understanding that sometimes witness orders change. But we will try and do that. I think it's a perfectly reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We might as well finalise that by now. The Trial Chamber had in mind that you would, after Wednesday, be in a position to indicate your first two weeks' of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, My Lord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And progressively after that you would proceed week by week so that you were in effect always roughly two weeks ahead with what you then anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My Lord, we are prepared to do that. Can I just please explain it is not always easy to get witnesses here but we as a matter of principle will endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that there will be understanding on their part just as you will have understanding when it becomes their turn if a witness presents a particular difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, My Lord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From the Chamber's point of view as long as we have a witness and can keep moving that will facilitate the eventual close of the case. So, Mr. Lukic, you have had your persuasive way. Everybody seems content that we will a two-week notification of the coming witnesses and that should facilitate both the Defence during the Prosecution case and the Prosecution during the Defence case. Is there any problem that any Defence counsel wishes to raise now about disclosure or is disclosure under control at this stage? If nobody rises, we will assume that there is no problem. Very good. Thank you for that. It's already been mentioned that the expert reports which were required under Rule 94 bis have now been provided, certainly in English. Are they all now provided in B/C/S, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to General Pringle, I brief the B/C/S was disclosed last Friday. In relation to Theunens report, that will require, I believe, another five days and will not be disclosed until approximately the 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will then complete the B/C/S disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware. May I just clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, everything is as I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. It does mean that about a week before the commencement of evidence all your expert reports will be disclosed in B/C/S as well as English. I see no reason to ask for any further comment from the Defence there. We have mentioned agreed facts and encourage both sides to pursue their efforts in that regard. The Chamber is aware that there is the outstanding motion to do with Rule 92 bis which has just been filed, which we have yet to see, and we will for our part, as soon as we have both the motion and the Defence response, be in a position to deal with it quickly. The Prosecution motion under Rule 65 ter should be published, filed today, and that will enable that to be dealt with. There is a motion of the Prosecution concerning protective measures. That decision -- we have the Defence response, and that decision will be filed in a few days' time. So that it should be that before the commencement of evidence all the presently outstanding motions are dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Mr. Moore, that you would wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My Lord, there are one or two small matters, perhaps more housekeeping than anything else. My learned friends have indicated quite reasonably that they well be wishing to cross-examine the witnesses who have given evidence on previous occasions, for example, either the Dokmanovic or Milosevic trials. Clearly if there's going to be cross-examination on statements whether for -- well, obviously for inconsistency, I can imagine that that will require a large amount of photocopying. Can we take it that the Defence will undertake to photocopy that material and provide it to the Court, because clearly they know the material that they will be dealing with, we don't. So can I just have that clarified, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before I turn to the Defence, from the Chamber's point of view if a counsel intends to cross-examine on a document, the Chamber would expect that counsel to have copies of that document ready for the Chamber, other counsel, and for the witness. Now, with that indication, is there anything that you would wish to add, any member of the Defence team? Mr. Vasic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on behalf of all the Defence team, precisely what you said. That is what the Defence thinks too. We share your opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's one part of the house tidy, Mr. Moore. Did I understand there was more than one you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I think actually that will be sufficient at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you, then. Well, there seems to be no other matter that needs to be raised now. We have deliberately left some matters in the air, and we will watch them closely and as necessary, and when it becomes practical to do it, it may be necessary for the Chamber to make more formal orders. But in the meantime, we look forward to opening submissions tomorrow from you, Mr. Moore, and the continuation of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is one matter. I had placed in front of yourselves the file. Because we will be going on an electronic procedure called Sanction, hopefully it will achieve what it sets out to do, I will be relying on those files in hard copy. They're not quite complete, and my learned friends will also be provided with copies of that. And additionally there will be copies of maps for the Court and my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. There being no other matter, we will then adjourn until 10.00 tomorrow when the case will formally commence. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: at 3.57 p.m.
